SPEAR-PHISING: THE LATEST CYBER CRIME

By: Nicky Troll | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Cyber Criminals target and make off with hundreds of thousands of rands in fraudulent electronic transfers by intercepting emails in sophisticated impersonation scam.

Unique Selling Point:
• GLOBAL CRIME TREND
• SOUTH AFRICANS LOSING MILLIONS
• AFFECTS EVERY INDUSTRY YOU CAN IMAGINE
• NICE CONSUMER EDUCATION PIECE
• VISUALLY INTERESTING WITH CYBER TECH / HACKER TYPE VISUALS


Summary:
With hundreds of millions of rands being transferred across bank accounts every single day in South Africa – cyber criminals are using advanced email hacking techniques to get their hands on the cash. Everyone is a target - from lawyers to small businesses to individuals – if there’s money moving, hackers are in the shadows, ready to intercept, impersonate and make with your hard earned cash.

We investigate this growing trend and ask who’s liable?


Further information:
THE TREND
Cyber Criminals are getting more sophisticated - targeting their attacks to deliver big bounties. It’s called Spear-Phising and it represents a serious for every industry imaginable. Spear-Phising is the fraudulent practice of sending emails ostensibly from a known or trusted sender in order to induce targeted individuals to reveal confidential information. Anyone and everyone doing electronic financial transactions is a potential target.

LET’S TALK FIGURES
South Africa faces an ever-evolving range of cyber threats ranking 3rd globally when it comes to the number of cybercrime victims. We’re talking an estimated R2.2 billion a year loss for local consumers and business.

26 percent of cybercrime in SA stems from electronic transfer fraud - which is 14 percent above the global average.
Impersonation attacks are up 62% globally and up by 37% in SA - this is emails impersonate a trusted individual or company in an attempt to gain access to corporate finances or data or to intercept funds with fake banking details.
HOW DO THEY DO IT
Cybercriminals have well-structured syndicates that have an aura of authenticity. They rely on email or WhatsApp - where you don’t question the validity of communication from contacts you know. They abuse the systems we trust and use for work or personal life. “As the world becomes more digitised, risks of exposure to cybercrime also increase.

SOUTH AFRICA NOT EQUIPPED
Companies have taken steps to protect themselves against an increasingly sophisticated global industry. However, South Africa is behind more developed nations. Although other countries have acknowledged the risks and built higher walls and electric fences, we’re still using picket fences because we ignore or are unaware of the changing risk patterns. While the regulatory frameworks abroad make it easier to prosecute cybercriminals, our Cybercrimes Bill is yet to become law. This is partly why it’s difficult to police and prosecute cybercriminals.

90% OF CYBERCRIME ATTACKS START WITH EMAIL
Business email is one of the most common platforms for cybercrime - nine out of 10 attacks start with email. The criminals use it to conduct the scam by pretending to be someone else. When a payment is due, the payer is sent a last minute email alleging to be from the receiver of the payment, requesting that the banking details be changed.
The differences in the email may be extremely subtle, for example substituting a "1" for an "I", or a name like "Petersen" may be spelled "Pietersen" in an email. In a high-pressure environment, mistakes may be overlooked easily. It could also be that the hacked person’s email is diverted to the crooks and the actual email address is used. There are many modus operandi’s but the result is always the same - the money is gone! Often the fraudulent transactions is only picked days later when the person expecting money is still empty handed – by that time the cyber crooks have moved the stolen money out of the bank account they supplied.
CONVEYANCERS PRIME TARGETS
Globally attorneys are particularly vulnerable to spear phishing / impersonation attacks because they deal in high value EFTs almost daily.

In South Africa, the fraud became so rife that in July 2016, the Attorneys Insurance Indemnity Fund - a non-profit company now called the Legal Practitioners Indemnity Insurance Fund, which provides indemnity insurance to all practicing attorneys in South Africa - excluded cybercrime from their cover.

A year later, the Fund’s general manager, Thomas Harban, reported that since that exclusion, the Fund had been notified of more than 50 cybercrime-related claims with a total value of more than R25 million. Two years on and that number has leapt to a staggering 133 claims with a total value of R83 million, again, all rejected.

WHERE DOES THE MONEY GO? MONEY MULES!
Like in our Tender Fraud story – the bank accounts are legitimately opened by an unsuspecting person who gives the criminals the account details for a fee. We can trace one of these accounts again, but there are costs attached. I would suggest doing that bank account search to find the money mule.

WHO’s FAULT IS IT AND WHO SHOULD TAKE RESPONSIBILITY?
Both parties! But in the majority of the cases it is legally tricky – because the person that was hacked is not always the person that the misrepresentation was made to and therefore not the person that was defrauded. It’s a fascinating discussion from a legal perspective.



CASE STUDY 1 – Jason Goliath - JHB
In 2018, Goliath and Goliath lost more than R300 000 to hackers. The cyber-criminals gained access to the company's emails and requested clients to make payments to a different bank account. They’re a prime example of small businesses being targetted by this crime trend. He is a well known personality that will lift our piece.


CASE STUDY 2 - Keri Murphy – CAPE TOWN
When the conveyancing attorney phoned her to discuss the transfer papers she would be sending, she had no idea that a fraudster had already been in contact with her via email, pretending to be her.

“He had altered my email address, but only slightly so she would not notice. I then received an email from the fraudster posing as the conveyancer. Her company header and email address had also been slightly altered, but as this was the first email I’d received from “the law firm”, I had no way of knowing that the email was not actually from them.”

The fraudster had inserted his own banking details in that email, and that’s how Murphy came to transfer almost R118 000 into the his bank account. Ten days later she got another call from the conveyancer, saying that no funds were reflecting in her bank account.

Murphy feels that the attorney - Anesta Kruger of Kruger & Blignaut Attorneys in Bredasdrop - is responsible because during that initial phone call, the subject of email hacking fraud - and the need to double-check email addresses and bank account details - was not raised by her at all.

And it was only after Murphy’s loss that Kruger added this line to all her correspondence: “Please note: Due to an increase in ongoing cyber and electronic fraud, you are obliged to personally verify our banking details, before making any payments to our firm. We will not accept any liability for any payments made to fraudulent bank accounts.”

The attorney told Murphy that the email breach was not on her side, and that “an attorney cannot foresee and advise clients on each and every possible crime or scenario, relating to a situation as this.”

LEGALLY SPEAKING In this case, the attorney’s emails were hacked. And the client was the one defrauded.


CASE STUDY 3: Lynne Marshall – CAPE TOWN

Last September (2017) a Cape Town-based conveyancing firm of attorneys, Botha & Venter Attorneys, fell for a scam email pretending to be from her client, Lynne Marshall - with a last-minute request that the R420 000 proceeds from the sale of her Muizenberg house be transferred into another bank account.

She did the transfer without doing any of the widely publicised recommended checks, and then refused to take responsibility for the loss.

"We had a written instruction to the conveyancers, on June 23, to pay the proceeds of the sale into my Absa account. After our bond was settled, that amounted to R420 000.
On Monday September 11, I emailed the conveyancers to say that no money was reflecting in my bank account as expected. In response, attorney Ronelle Botha’s PA emailed me proof of payment. And that’s how I discovered that our money had been paid not into our Absa account, but into a Nedbank account. It emerged that a week earlier, hours after I phoned Botha & Venter to query the transfer - a call in which I made no mention of a change in my banking details - the practice had received what it thought was an email from her, requesting that the money be paid into a Nedbank account. The email address used was very similar to mine.”

The Marshalls are currently suing the attorney.

LEGALLY SPEAKING When there is fraud – a misrepresentation is made and the mark is defrauded. In this case, the misreprestation was made to the attorney. The attorney was defrauded – not the client.

ELEMENTS
THREE STRONG CASE STUDIES
Demonstrating different scenarios

CYBER CRIME EXPERT: Danny Myburgh
Will explain the MO and what people should look out for
Investigates about 4 of these cases every week

LEGAL EXPERT: Zaakir Mohammed at Cliff Dekker Hoffmeyer Attorneys
Will explain the legal challenges and responsibility of cyber crime cases.

FINDING THE MONEY MULE

I don’t think we need to interview the Fidelit Fund – that’s a link. Also don’t think we need SABRIC – it’s also just a link and the banks do nothing because the transactions were valid even though the details weren’t

• EXTRA HALF with the presenter because we’d need to cover at least a day and a half shoot in JHB with filming a case study, experts and tracking the money mule.

Press Release:


Cyber Impersonation Scam
From your bank account details to your home address – your emails hold a treasure trove of personal information about you and every transaction you make can be traced right back to your electronic signature. Every day in South Africa people transfer and receive funds, using the internet and from the comfort of their own homes – but where there’s money moving, criminals aren’t far behind. Now, by intercepting and impersonating you on your emails, cyber hackers are making off with thousands of rands in fraudulent electronic transfers. Carte Blanche investigates.
Producer: Nicky Troll
Presenter: Devi Sankaree Govender
Watch the trailer


Script:


IMPERSONATION SCAM STRUCTURE

VO: We live in an exceedingly digitized world where the cyber realm is a prime hunting ground for fraudsters who are masters of deception.

LINK: The risk for exposure in the digital underworld is higher than you think. Every single industry that does financial transactions electronically - is at risk. Don’t be fooled - everyone is target – even you.
UPSOUND AWEH
VO: Comedian Jason Goliath’s business got scammed out of R285 thousand rand in a sophisticated impersonation cyber scam – without his company even realising it.

JASON: // people that thought they never got robbed got robbed. // a grown 38 year old human, I got conned.

VO: Professional Cyber criminals operate behind a veil of anonymity, cloaked with authenticity.

LINK: Gone are the days of crooks using far fetched story lines – people have wised up to the stock standard 419 scams, romance cons and those big lottery wins. Cyber criminals have upped their game and hooking victims in real life business transactions.

VO: First, email communication will be compromised, the crooks then intercept financial transactions by pretending to be you or the other party who is known to you, they change the intended banking details to theirs and make off with the money while the victims think it was a legitimate transaction.

JASON: now you check the proof of payment – but these are not my banking details DEVI: but in your name? //
JASON: in my name // different bank account number.

VO: In Jason’s case – cyber criminals intercepted multiple invoices due to the company - conning their clients into thinking they were dealing with Goliath & Goliath – the crooks even intercepted a R60 000 invoice that Jason ended up paying twice – once to the crooks and then to the right people.

JASON: At the time basically every single invoice that was sent out from anybody in the office was tracked and intercepted // we could have lost everything to somebody who doesn’t even know how I look.

VO: South Africa has the third highest number of cyber crime victims in the world - with this type of Impersonation attacks up by 37% in the country last year.

DEVI: Why fall for this?
DANNY: // you are expecting the transaction, // They are not scanning anybody, they first get information that there is a transaction that is about to happen then they start focussing on the parties involved.

VO: Cyber security expert, Danny Myburgh believes we are dealing with sophisticated syndicates, executing well-orchestrated attacks using social engineering and meticulous planning.

The tactics are vast - from hackers lurking on unprotected wifi networks, to phising links and spyware – but the motive stays the same – get to the money.

One of the hardest hit industries is the legal fraternity.

DANNY: // the syndicates knows that there’s constant communication between them and their clients, they know they are holding money in trust, and they know that there is a large through put of transactions //INT1 M28

VO: Keri Murphy was involved in one of these big ticket transactions in April this year. She paid just over R110 thousand rand for a deposit and some conveyancing fees for a piece of land in Tesselaarsdal in the Western Cape.

KERI: // I went into the bank and did the transfer, and I got my proof of payment and I sent it to the conveyancing attorneys // only 10 days later 16 April – she was bit weary money still hadn’t cleared.

VO: Keri’s R110 thousand rand had been transferred into the cyber criminals account – the money was gone.

The fraudsters intercepted the original invoice from the conveyancer, inserted a different bank account on the document and sent that to Keri instead. She never received the original invoice.

KERI: I just trusted in good faith that this was the right bank details - I have never heard of these phising scams // it was completely authentic in my minds eye.

VO: In this case, the fraudsters sent both Keri and the conveyancer emails from fake addresses impersonating both parties.

DANNY: // they falsify the mail, they make a small change to it – put a 1 behind, misspell a name etc. // they will also just have the display name that says Danny Myburgh for example – you don’t actually see the email where it is going to.

VO: Often the only trail to follow – is the money – we picked up on Keri’s case.

LINK: The account belongs to a company called Thu Infrastructure – the address we’ve traced to Sunnyside, but there is a sole director and the sole director is a Mr Mabona.

VO: While the address is real, it appeared that no one was home, so we called the number we had on record.

DEVI: Hello Mr Mabona?
SLEG: Yes
DEVI: Is that Sleg Edward Mabona?
SLEG: Yes
DEVI: Is your name Sleg, like S L E G, sleg - like the Afrikaans?
SLEG: yes
DEVI: Ok Shame.
DEVI: where do you live?
SLEG: I’m in Mpumalanga…
DEVI: …money went in, part of cyber fraud, R110k bank account that’s registered in your name
SLEG: // I lost everything, my bank card, my id was taken away from me.
DEVI: When was that?
SLEG: 3 – 4 months back //not good for someone to use my details – eish! I don’t know

VO: As we left we bumped into the actual tenant staying at the address.

DEVI: DO you know Sleg Edward Mabona?
TENANT: no, first time I’m hearing it from you. I don’t know this person.
DEVI: This is not your bank account, this nedbank account?
TENANT: no, no, it’s not – everything here – is new to me – except that I know this address because I live, where I stay.

VO: But our investigation revealed that Sleg Edward wasn’t completely honest with us.

LINK: SLeg Edward Mabona – you heard him he said he’s in Mpumalange – he’s not – he’s in Mamelodi

SLEG: I say now I’m not in Mamelodi.
DEVI: you are in Mamelodi now – I know for a fact you are in mamelodi – I’m asking why did you are lie to me?
SLEG: I’m in trouble ne?
DEVI: What else lying about
SLEG: where can we meet?

VO: We waited for him, but alas, he was a no show.

LINK: Once the money reflects in the criminal account – it gets moved almost instantly, split over different accounts to spread the risk of detection and eventually the cash will be drawn out at ATMs, by multiple runners.

ZAAKIR: This is their business, this is how they make money, by defrauding people out of hundreds of thousands of rands – they are on top of technology.

VO: Attorney Zaakir Mohammed says these legally complex cases fall both into a criminal and civil category.

ZAAKIR: You have to look at each case based on it’s own merits, there is no, you know, winning formula when it comes to this kind of thing, // not just nationally, but globally as well.

VO: In most cases, all parties involved would have unknowingly played a role on some level in making the con a success, Mohamed explains assigning blame and liability is no simple task.

ZAAKIR: there are many factors that would come into play in assessing the merits of your case, you would have to assess the evidence, you would have to look at your IT systems, you would also have to look at the quantum of your loss, is it something that you think you would be able to recover.

VO: But this can result in lengthy legal battles as Lynne Marshall and Rick Lawrence have learnt. In September 2017, their conveyancer paid the profits of a property sale into the wrong bank account – R420 thousand rand – GONE!

LYNNE: If that had been our only savings, if we had sold // and we had nothing else – what would you do – you would be suicidal – it’s just all wrong.

VO: The conveyancer received an email from a fake email address instructing them to change the banking details for the money due to Lynne and Rick.

LYNNE: This is what I can’t understand – email on day of transfer – change – she doesn’t pick up the phone to say is this right.

VO: In July 2016, the Legal practitioners Fidelity Fund excluded cybercrime from their insurance cover - rejecting a staggering 110 claims with a total value of exceeding R85 million to date.

LYNNE: It seems to me that nobody has taken notice of it – they don’t say to you that you may be at risk, they don’t offer you the opportunity to take out insurance so that you could be covered // they take no responsibility what so ever.

VO: As for the banks they claim their hands are tied saying that the actual transaction was lawful even though the recipient appears to be a fraudster.

With no one taking any liability – Lynne, Keri and Jason are still out of pocket.

JASON: we innocently believe because we are law-abiding citizens and we’d never take a chance with the bank, that nobody else would.

VO: In Lynne, Jason and Keri’s cases the bank account holder name did not match the bank account number.

This is how it works… fraudsters will have a bank account number in the name of say JOHN SMITH. But they then use YOUR name with JOHN SMITH’s account number – making the person doing the payment think it’s legit. The bank doesn’t blocked or even flag the transaction despite this glaring inaccuracy – it goes through and the money is gone.

DANNY: I think that this one of the simplest things that the financial institutions can help with the banks, that if the money is supposed to go into Danny Myburgh’s account - it should be Danny Myburgh’s account and nobody else.

VO: The Payment Association of South Africa regulates payments – they make the rules, develop strategies and ensure enforcement. Walter Volker is the CEO.

WALTER: if you look at the payment system it’s always a balance between - risk and fraud management vs convenience and cost – you will pay more and inconvenience the customer.

JASON: //Its definitely not as inconvenient as R285k. // At least give them one more hurdle to climb over, at the moment – to rob you, all these guys need to do is change one line on any invoice you’ve ever sent – they change that banking detail line – and you’re done// DO you know how hard it is to write a joke, all I need to do is write a number.

DEVI:…. isn’t rocket science it’s obvious
WALTER: There is no country in the world that verifies the name of the beneficiary.

VO: Volker says future projects could address these issues, but the process won’t be quick as it depends on what technology permits.

Currently some banks offer online account verification – it’s not an automatic service and comes at a fee – you will also need the person’s ID number or company registration information and contact details.

In the meantime, anyone making electronic payments should be on high alert and verify every single detail before clicking pay.

KERI: I wish I had the money under my bed and taken it over and paid it in cash rather than doing a transfer. // I am terrified // you think you’re in this digital world and we’re progressing and we’re going three steps back.


PROMOS
PROMO 1
VO: Cyber Criminals target and make off with hundreds of thousands of rands in fraudulent electronic transfers by intercepting emails in a sophisticated impersonation scam.

PROMO 2
VO: With hundreds of millions of rands being moved across bank accounts every day in South Africa – cyber criminals are using advanced email hacking techniques to get their hands on your cash.

PROMO 3
VO: Imagine doing a bank transfer – but the money doesn’t reach the recipient – you paid it into the wrong account because hackers sent you their banking details in intercepted email communication.

We will not accept any liability for any payments made to fraudulent bank accounts.” The attorney told Murphy that the email breach was not on her side, and that “an attorney cannot foresee and advise clients on each and every possible crime or scenario, relating to a situation as this.” LEGALLY SPEAKING In this case, the attorney’s emails were hacked. And the client was the one defrauded. CASE STUDY 3: Lynne Marshall – CAPE TOWN Last September (2017) a Cape Town-based conveyancing firm of attorneys, Botha & Venter Attorneys, fell for a scam email pretending to be from her client, Lynne Marshall - with a last-minute request that the R420 000 proceeds from the sale of her Muizenberg house be transferred into another bank account. She did the transfer without doing any of the widely publicised recommended checks, and then refused to take responsibility for the loss. "We had a written instruction to the conveyancers, on June 23, to pay the proceeds of the sale into my Absa account. After our bond was settled, that amounted to R420 000. On Monday September 11, I emailed the conveyancers to say that no money was reflecting in my bank account as expected. In response, attorney Ronelle Botha’s PA emailed me proof of payment. And that’s how I discovered that our money had been paid not into our Absa account, but into a Nedbank account. It emerged that a week earlier, hours after I phoned Botha & Venter to query the transfer - a call in which I made no mention of a change in my banking details - the practice had received what it thought was an email from her, requesting that the money be paid into a Nedbank account. The email address used was very similar to mine.” The Marshalls are currently suing the attorney. LEGALLY SPEAKING When there is fraud – a misrepresentation is made and the mark is defrauded. In this case, the misreprestation was made to the attorney. The attorney was defrauded – not the client. Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 29 July 2019 Press Release: Cyber Impersonation Scam From your bank account details to your home address – your emails hold a treasure trove of personal information about you and every transaction you make can be traced right back to your electronic signature. Every day in South Africa people transfer and receive funds, using the internet and from the comfort of their own homes – but where there’s money moving, criminals aren’t far behind. Now, by intercepting and impersonating you on your emails, cyber hackers are making off with thousands of rands in fraudulent electronic transfers. Carte Blanche investigates. Producer: Nicky Troll Presenter: Devi Sankaree Govender Watch the trailer Script: IMPERSONATION SCAM STRUCTURE VO: We live in an exceedingly digitized world where the cyber realm is a prime hunting ground for fraudsters who are masters of deception. LINK: The risk for exposure in the digital underworld is higher than you think. Every single industry that does financial transactions electronically - is at risk. Don’t be fooled - everyone is target – even you. UPSOUND AWEH VO: Comedian Jason Goliath’s business got scammed out of R285 thousand rand in a sophisticated impersonation cyber scam – without his company even realising it. JASON: // people that thought they never got robbed got robbed. // a grown 38 year old human, I got conned. VO: Professional Cyber criminals operate behind a veil of anonymity, cloaked with authenticity. LINK: Gone are the days of crooks using far fetched story lines – people have wised up to the stock standard 419 scams, romance cons and those big lottery wins. Cyber criminals have upped their game and hooking victims in real life business transactions. VO: First, email communication will be compromised, the crooks then intercept financial transactions by pretending to be you or the other party who is known to you, they change the intended banking details to theirs and make off with the money while the victims think it was a legitimate transaction. JASON: now you check the proof of payment – but these are not my banking details DEVI: but in your name? // JASON: in my name // different bank account number. VO: In Jason’s case – cyber criminals intercepted multiple invoices due to the company - conning their clients into thinking they were dealing with Goliath & Goliath – the crooks even intercepted a R60 000 invoice that Jason ended up paying twice – once to the crooks and then to the right people. JASON: At the time basically every single invoice that was sent out from anybody in the office was tracked and intercepted // we could have lost everything to somebody who doesn’t even know how I look. VO: South Africa has the third highest number of cyber crime victims in the world - with this type of Impersonation attacks up by 37% in the country last year. DEVI: Why fall for this? DANNY: // you are expecting the transaction, // They are not scanning anybody, they first get information that there is a transaction that is about to happen then they start focussing on the parties involved. VO: Cyber security expert, Danny Myburgh believes we are dealing with sophisticated syndicates, executing well-orchestrated attacks using social engineering and meticulous planning. The tactics are vast - from hackers lurking on unprotected wifi networks, to phising links and spyware – but the motive stays the same – get to the money. One of the hardest hit industries is the legal fraternity. DANNY: // the syndicates knows that there’s constant communication between them and their clients, they know they are holding money in trust, and they know that there is a large through put of transactions //INT1 M28 VO: Keri Murphy was involved in one of these big ticket transactions in April this year. She paid just over R110 thousand rand for a deposit and some conveyancing fees for a piece of land in Tesselaarsdal in the Western Cape. KERI: // I went into the bank and did the transfer, and I got my proof of payment and I sent it to the conveyancing attorneys // only 10 days later 16 April – she was bit weary money still hadn’t cleared. VO: Keri’s R110 thousand rand had been transferred into the cyber criminals account – the money was gone. The fraudsters intercepted the original invoice from the conveyancer, inserted a different bank account on the document and sent that to Keri instead. She never received the original invoice. KERI: I just trusted in good faith that this was the right bank details - I have never heard of these phising scams // it was completely authentic in my minds eye. VO: In this case, the fraudsters sent both Keri and the conveyancer emails from fake addresses impersonating both parties. DANNY: // they falsify the mail, they make a small change to it – put a 1 behind, misspell a name etc. // they will also just have the display name that says Danny Myburgh for example – you don’t actually see the email where it is going to. VO: Often the only trail to follow – is the money – we picked up on Keri’s case. LINK: The account belongs to a company called Thu Infrastructure – the address we’ve traced to Sunnyside, but there is a sole director and the sole director is a Mr Mabona. VO: While the address is real, it appeared that no one was home, so we called the number we had on record. DEVI: Hello Mr Mabona? SLEG: Yes DEVI: Is that Sleg Edward Mabona? SLEG: Yes DEVI: Is your name Sleg, like S L E G, sleg - like the Afrikaans? SLEG: yes DEVI: Ok Shame. DEVI: where do you live? SLEG: I’m in Mpumalanga… DEVI: …money went in, part of cyber fraud, R110k bank account that’s registered in your name SLEG: // I lost everything, my bank card, my id was taken away from me. DEVI: When was that? SLEG: 3 – 4 months back //not good for someone to use my details – eish! I don’t know VO: As we left we bumped into the actual tenant staying at the address. DEVI: DO you know Sleg Edward Mabona? TENANT: no, first time I’m hearing it from you. I don’t know this person. DEVI: This is not your bank account, this nedbank account? TENANT: no, no, it’s not – everything here – is new to me – except that I know this address because I live, where I stay. VO: But our investigation revealed that Sleg Edward wasn’t completely honest with us. LINK: SLeg Edward Mabona – you heard him he said he’s in Mpumalange – he’s not – he’s in Mamelodi SLEG: I say now I’m not in Mamelodi. DEVI: you are in Mamelodi now – I know for a fact you are in mamelodi – I’m asking why did you are lie to me? SLEG: I’m in trouble ne? DEVI: What else lying about SLEG: where can we meet? VO: We waited for him, but alas, he was a no show. LINK: Once the money reflects in the criminal account – it gets moved almost instantly, split over different accounts to spread the risk of detection and eventually the cash will be drawn out at ATMs, by multiple runners. ZAAKIR: This is their business, this is how they make money, by defrauding people out of hundreds of thousands of rands – they are on top of technology. VO: Attorney Zaakir Mohammed says these legally complex cases fall both into a criminal and civil category. ZAAKIR: You have to look at each case based on it’s own merits, there is no, you know, winning formula when it comes to this kind of thing, // not just nationally, but globally as well. VO: In most cases, all parties involved would have unknowingly played a role on some level in making the con a success, Mohamed explains assigning blame and liability is no simple task. ZAAKIR: there are many factors that would come into play in assessing the merits of your case, you would have to assess the evidence, you would have to look at your IT systems, you would also have to look at the quantum of your loss, is it something that you think you would be able to recover. VO: But this can result in lengthy legal battles as Lynne Marshall and Rick Lawrence have learnt. In September 2017, their conveyancer paid the profits of a property sale into the wrong bank account – R420 thousand rand – GONE! LYNNE: If that had been our only savings, if we had sold // and we had nothing else – what would you do – you would be suicidal – it’s just all wrong. VO: The conveyancer received an email from a fake email address instructing them to change the banking details for the money due to Lynne and Rick. LYNNE: This is what I can’t understand – email on day of transfer – change – she doesn’t pick up the phone to say is this right. VO: In July 2016, the Legal practitioners Fidelity Fund excluded cybercrime from their insurance cover - rejecting a staggering 110 claims with a total value of exceeding R85 million to date. LYNNE: It seems to me that nobody has taken notice of it – they don’t say to you that you may be at risk, they don’t offer you the opportunity to take out insurance so that you could be covered // they take no responsibility what so ever. VO: As for the banks they claim their hands are tied saying that the actual transaction was lawful even though the recipient appears to be a fraudster. With no one taking any liability – Lynne, Keri and Jason are still out of pocket. JASON: we innocently believe because we are law-abiding citizens and we’d never take a chance with the bank, that nobody else would. VO: In Lynne, Jason and Keri’s cases the bank account holder name did not match the bank account number. This is how it works… fraudsters will have a bank account number in the name of say JOHN SMITH. But they then use YOUR name with JOHN SMITH’s account number – making the person doing the payment think it’s legit. The bank doesn’t blocked or even flag the transaction despite this glaring inaccuracy – it goes through and the money is gone. DANNY: I think that this one of the simplest things that the financial institutions can help with the banks, that if the money is supposed to go into Danny Myburgh’s account - it should be Danny Myburgh’s account and nobody else. VO: The Payment Association of South Africa regulates payments – they make the rules, develop strategies and ensure enforcement. Walter Volker is the CEO. WALTER: if you look at the payment system it’s always a balance between - risk and fraud management vs convenience and cost – you will pay more and inconvenience the customer. JASON: //Its definitely not as inconvenient as R285k. // At least give them one more hurdle to climb over, at the moment – to rob you, all these guys need to do is change one line on any invoice you’ve ever sent – they change that banking detail line – and you’re done// DO you know how hard it is to write a joke, all I need to do is write a number. DEVI:…. isn’t rocket science it’s obvious WALTER: There is no country in the world that verifies the name of the beneficiary. VO: Volker says future projects could address these issues, but the process won’t be quick as it depends on what technology permits. Currently some banks offer online account verification – it’s not an automatic service and comes at a fee – you will also need the person’s ID number or company registration information and contact details. In the meantime, anyone making electronic payments should be on high alert and verify every single detail before clicking pay. KERI: I wish I had the money under my bed and taken it over and paid it in cash rather than doing a transfer. // I am terrified // you think you’re in this digital world and we’re progressing and we’re going three steps back. PROMOS PROMO 1 VO: Cyber Criminals target and make off with hundreds of thousands of rands in fraudulent electronic transfers by intercepting emails in a sophisticated impersonation scam. PROMO 2 VO: With hundreds of millions of rands being moved across bank accounts every day in South Africa – cyber criminals are using advanced email hacking techniques to get their hands on your cash. PROMO 3 VO: Imagine doing a bank transfer – but the money doesn’t reach the recipient – you paid it into the wrong account because hackers sent you their banking details in intercepted email communication.

metadata.Summary: With hundreds of millions of rands being transferred across bank accounts every single day in South Africa – cyber criminals are using advanced email hacking techniques to get their hands on the cash. Everyone is a target - from lawyers to small businesses to individuals – if there’s money moving, hackers are in the shadows, ready to intercept, impersonate and make with your hard earned cash. We investigate this growing trend and ask who’s liable?
metadata.Further information: THE TREND Cyber Criminals are getting more sophisticated - targeting their attacks to deliver big bounties. It’s called Spear-Phising and it represents a serious for every industry imaginable. Spear-Phising is the fraudulent practice of sending emails ostensibly from a known or trusted sender in order to induce targeted individuals to reveal confidential information. Anyone and everyone doing electronic financial transactions is a potential target. LET’S TALK FIGURES South Africa faces an ever-evolving range of cyber threats ranking 3rd globally when it comes to the number of cybercrime victims. We’re talking an estimated R2.2 billion a year loss for local consumers and business. 26 percent of cybercrime in SA stems from electronic transfer fraud - which is 14 percent above the global average. Impersonation attacks are up 62% globally and up by 37% in SA - this is emails impersonate a trusted individual or company in an attempt to gain access to corporate finances or data or to intercept funds with fake banking details. HOW DO THEY DO IT Cybercriminals have well-structured syndicates that have an aura of authenticity. They rely on email or WhatsApp - where you don’t question the validity of communication from contacts you know. They abuse the systems we trust and use for work or personal life. “As the world becomes more digitised, risks of exposure to cybercrime also increase. SOUTH AFRICA NOT EQUIPPED Companies have taken steps to protect themselves against an increasingly sophisticated global industry. However, South Africa is behind more developed nations. Although other countries have acknowledged the risks and built higher walls and electric fences, we’re still using picket fences because we ignore or are unaware of the changing risk patterns. While the regulatory frameworks abroad make it easier to prosecute cybercriminals, our Cybercrimes Bill is yet to become law. This is partly why it’s difficult to police and prosecute cybercriminals. 90% OF CYBERCRIME ATTACKS START WITH EMAIL Business email is one of the most common platforms for cybercrime - nine out of 10 attacks start with email. The criminals use it to conduct the scam by pretending to be someone else. When a payment is due, the payer is sent a last minute email alleging to be from the receiver of the payment, requesting that the banking details be changed. The differences in the email may be extremely subtle, for example substituting a "1" for an "I", or a name like "Petersen" may be spelled "Pietersen" in an email. In a high-pressure environment, mistakes may be overlooked easily. It could also be that the hacked person’s email is diverted to the crooks and the actual email address is used. There are many modus operandi’s but the result is always the same - the money is gone! Often the fraudulent transactions is only picked days later when the person expecting money is still empty handed – by that time the cyber crooks have moved the stolen money out of the bank account they supplied. CONVEYANCERS PRIME TARGETS Globally attorneys are particularly vulnerable to spear phishing / impersonation attacks because they deal in high value EFTs almost daily. In South Africa, the fraud became so rife that in July 2016, the Attorneys Insurance Indemnity Fund - a non-profit company now called the Legal Practitioners Indemnity Insurance Fund, which provides indemnity insurance to all practicing attorneys in South Africa - excluded cybercrime from their cover. A year later, the Fund’s general manager, Thomas Harban, reported that since that exclusion, the Fund had been notified of more than 50 cybercrime-related claims with a total value of more than R25 million. Two years on and that number has leapt to a staggering 133 claims with a total value of R83 million, again, all rejected. WHERE DOES THE MONEY GO? MONEY MULES! Like in our Tender Fraud story – the bank accounts are legitimately opened by an unsuspecting person who gives the criminals the account details for a fee. We can trace one of these accounts again, but there are costs attached. I would suggest doing that bank account search to find the money mule. WHO’s FAULT IS IT AND WHO SHOULD TAKE RESPONSIBILITY? Both parties! But in the majority of the cases it is legally tricky – because the person that was hacked is not always the person that the misrepresentation was made to and therefore not the person that was defrauded. It’s a fascinating discussion from a legal perspective. CASE STUDY 1 – Jason Goliath - JHB In 2018, Goliath and Goliath lost more than R300 000 to hackers. The cyber-criminals gained access to the company's emails and requested clients to make payments to a different bank account. They’re a prime example of small businesses being targetted by this crime trend. He is a well known personality that will lift our piece. CASE STUDY 2 - Keri Murphy – CAPE TOWN When the conveyancing attorney phoned her to discuss the transfer papers she would be sending, she had no idea that a fraudster had already been in contact with her via email, pretending to be her. “He had altered my email address, but only slightly so she would not notice. I then received an email from the fraudster posing as the conveyancer. Her company header and email address had also been slightly altered, but as this was the first email I’d received from “the law firm”, I had no way of knowing that the email was not actually from them.” The fraudster had inserted his own banking details in that email, and that’s how Murphy came to transfer almost R118 000 into the his bank account. We will not accept any liability for any payments made to fraudulent bank accounts.” The attorney told Murphy that the email breach was not on her side, and that “an attorney cannot foresee and advise clients on each and every possible crime or scenario, relating to a situation as this.” LEGALLY SPEAKING In this case, the attorney’s emails were hacked.
